content: The prevalence of substance use, both prescribed and non-prescribed, is increasing globally. Among women of childbearing age, substance use has contributed to rising rates of neonatal abstinence syndrome (NAS). Neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome (NOWS) is a term used to describe the subset of NAS specifically related to opioid exposure. Non-pharmacological care is considered the first-line treatment for managing substance withdrawal in newborns. However, there is no universally accepted definition or standard for non-pharmacological care practices in this population. Evaluating the safety and efficacy of these practices could provide clearer guidance for clinical care. The objective of this review was to assess the safety and efficacy of non-pharmacological treatments for infants at risk of, or showing symptoms consistent with, opioid withdrawal. Specifically, the review aimed to determine whether non-pharmacological care reduces the length of hospitalization and the need for pharmacological treatment. Additionally, it sought to evaluate whether combining non-pharmacological care with pharmacological treatment reduces the duration of pharmacological therapy, the maximum and cumulative doses of opioid medications, and the length of hospitalization. The search strategy included databases such as CENTRAL, Ovid MEDLINE, and CINAHL, as well as clinical trial registries and reference lists of retrieved articles. The search was conducted on October 11, 2019. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs), quasi-RCTs, and cluster trials that compared single or bundled non-pharmacological interventions to either no non-pharmacological treatment or other non-pharmacological interventions. Non-pharmacological interventions were categorized into three groups: modifying environmental stimulation, feeding practices, and supporting the mother-infant dyad. Non-randomized studies identified during the search were presented narratively. The review followed standard Cochrane methodological procedures and used the GRADE approach to assess the certainty of evidence. Primary outcomes for infants at risk of, or showing early symptoms of, opioid withdrawal included the length of hospitalization and the use of pharmacological treatment (defined as one or more doses of opioid or sedative medication). For infants already receiving pharmacological treatment for opioid withdrawal, primary outcomes included the length of hospitalization, the duration of pharmacological treatment, and the maximum and cumulative doses of opioid medication. Six RCTs involving 353 infants were identified, with studies conducted between 1975 and 2018. No RCTs were found that specifically included infants already receiving pharmacological treatment for opioid withdrawal. The certainty of evidence for all outcomes was rated as very low to low. Additionally, 34 non-randomized studies published between 2005 and 2018 were excluded, including 29 studies involving infants at risk of, or showing symptoms of, opioid withdrawal and five studies involving infants receiving pharmacological treatment. Seven preregistered interventional clinical trials were identified, which may qualify for inclusion in future updates of the review. Of the six RCTs, four studies evaluated interventions aimed at modifying environmental stimulation, such as the use of a mechanical rocking bed, prone positioning, a non-oscillating waterbed, or a low-stimulation nursery. One study assessed feeding practices by comparing 24 kcal/oz formula to 20 kcal/oz formula. Another study focused on supporting the maternal-infant dyad through tailored breastfeeding support. In terms of outcomes, there was no evidence of a difference in the length of hospitalization in the study assessing environmental stimulation (mean difference [MD] –1 day, 95% confidence interval [CI] –2.82 to 0.82; 30 infants; very low-certainty evidence) or in the study evaluating support of the maternal-infant dyad (MD –8.9 days, 95% CI –19.84 to 2.04; 14 infants; very low-certainty evidence). No studies on feeding practices evaluated the length of hospitalization. Similarly, there was no evidence of a difference in the use of pharmacological treatment in three studies of environmental stimulation (typical risk ratio [RR] 1.00, 95% CI 0.86 to 1.16; 92 infants; low-certainty evidence), one study of feeding practices (RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.63 to 1.33; 49 infants; very low-certainty evidence), or one study of support of the maternal-infant dyad (RR 0.50, 95% CI 0.13 to 1.90; 14 infants; very low-certainty evidence). Secondary outcomes included neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) admission, time to regain birth weight, and weight nadir. One study of maternal-infant dyad support reported NICU admission (RR 0.50, 95% CI 0.13 to 1.90; 14 infants; very low-certainty evidence). One study of feeding practices reported the time to regain birth weight (MD 1.10 days, 95% CI –2.76 to 0.56; 46 infants; very low-certainty evidence). Weight nadir was reported in one study of environmental stimulation (MD –0.28, 95% CI –1.15 to 0.59; 194 infants; very low-certainty evidence) and one study of feeding practices (MD –0.8, 95% CI –2.24 to 0.64; 46 infants; very low-certainty evidence). The authors concluded that there is insufficient evidence to determine whether non-pharmacological care for opioid withdrawal in newborns affects key clinical outcomes, such as the length of hospitalization and the use of pharmacological treatment. The evidence from the six included studies was of very low to low certainty. Combined analysis was limited by heterogeneity in study design, intervention definitions, and the small number of studies. Many prespecified outcomes were not reported. While experts recommend optimizing non-pharmacological care before initiating pharmacological treatment, there is currently insufficient evidence to guide specific clinical practices. Larger, well-designed studies are needed to evaluate the effects of non-pharmacological care for opioid withdrawal in newborns.
